In 2001 the Joint Commission declared patient pain as "the fifth vital sign." Doctors were expected to help patients deal with pain or else they were being negligent. That meant handing out pain pills because the other option was the threat of malpractice claims, already a huge drain on doctor time and money.

But opioids, when taken for an extended period of time, actually make pain worse. The patients don't know it, though. They get addicted to the painkillers and the painkillers induce hyperalgesia, and if the doctors finally cut them off, they get their fix from heroin and other opium-derived street drugs. And they just spiral down. I've heard that an overwhelming majority of drug overdoses are due to doctor-prescribed drugs, often dangerous interactions between different Rx drugs.

This is not even to get into how poorly many doctors understand and deal with patient addicts. Giving opioids to an addict is a horrifically bad idea that often plunges them back into their addictions and ultimately kills them. There are conflicting views on how to deal with addicts, with some doctors preferring replacement therapies (substituting a less dangerous controlled substance for the addict's illicit substance) and others advocating sobriety. Interesting to note that doctor addicts are ALWAYS pushed to get sober, never to live a half-life strung out on replacement drugs.

Anyway, TL;DR: yes, it's a problem. A problem caused ultimately, in my understanding, by threats of malpractice lawsuits and by poor doctor understanding of opioids and addiction.
